title: Governance at the State Level
summary: India is a federation with governments at the Union and State levels, each with an executive, legislature and judiciary on parliamentary lines. In the State, executive power is vested in the Governor, but the Governor is a nominal head; the real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister.

Appointment: by the President (in practice on the Prime Minister's advice). Qualifications: citizen of India, at least 35 years old, holding no office of profit. Term: five years, but holds office during the pleasure of the President, who may remove him/her earlier. One person may be Governor of two or more States.

Powers: (a) Executive — appoints the Chief Minister (the leader of the majority in the Assembly) and, on the CM's advice, other ministers; appoints the Advocate General, chairpersons and members of the State Public Service Commission, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission, and judges of courts below the High Court; is consulted when the President appoints High Court judges. (b) Legislative — summons and prorogues the legislature and can dissolve the Assembly; addresses it; may nominate one Anglo-Indian to the Assembly and one-sixth of the Legislative Council; a bill becomes law only with the Governor's assent. (c) Financial — the budget is presented on the Governor's behalf; no money bill without the Governor's recommendation; controls the State Contingency Fund. (d) Discretionary — chooses the Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority; may reserve a bill for the President; may report to the President that the State government is not working according to the Constitution, leading to President's Rule under Article 356, when the Governor rules on behalf of the President.

Relationship with the Council of Ministers: normally the Governor acts on its advice and is informed of all its decisions through the Chief Minister; ministers stay in office as long as they enjoy the Assembly's majority. Yet the Governor is not merely ceremonial — he/she becomes effective in political instability, as the link between the Centre and the State, and through discretionary powers.
## Chief Minister and Council of Ministers

The Chief Minister and ministers are appointed by the Governor for five years but stay only while they have majority support; a non-member must become an MLA or MLC within six months. The Chief Minister is the real head of the State government: advises the Governor on appointing ministers and allocates portfolios; presides over and coordinates the Council of Ministers; guides policies and approves bills; is the sole link between the Council of Ministers and the Governor; places a single minister's decision before the whole Council if the Governor wishes. The CM is most powerful with a clear majority; in a coalition government his/her role is limited by partners and independents.

Most States are unicameral (Legislative Assembly only); a few (e.g. Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) are bicameral with a Legislative Council. The Governor is part of the legislature.

Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha): 60–500 members (smaller in Goa, Sikkim, Mizoram), directly elected by universal adult franchise (all citizens 18 and above); seats reserved for SC and ST. An MLA must be a citizen, 25 years old, on the voters' list, not holding an office of profit or a government job. Term: five years (may be dissolved earlier, or extended by one year at a time in a national emergency).

Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad): not more than one-third of the Assembly's size and not less than 40 (Jammu & Kashmir's had 36). One-third elected by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers and one-sixth nominated by the Governor. It is a permanent house — never dissolved; members serve six years and one-third retire every two years. Minimum age 30. The legislature must meet at least twice a year (gap less than six months).

Functions: (a) Law-making — the Assembly has the final say; the Council can delay an ordinary bill but if the Assembly passes it again it is deemed passed; money bills start only in the Assembly and the Council must return them within 14 days; the Governor cannot refuse assent to a money bill but may return other bills or reserve them for the President. (b) Control over the executive — the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Assembly and can be removed by a no-confidence motion; questions, adjournment motions and calling-attention notices keep a check. (c) Electoral — elected MLAs vote in the election of the President and elect the State's Rajya Sabha members and one-third of the Legislative Council. (d) Constitutional amendments — some need ratification by half the State legislatures.

State governments run welfare schemes: residential bridge courses for out-of-school children in Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan; hot mid-day meals in over 95,000 primary schools in Uttar Pradesh; Maharashtra's School Sanitation and Hygiene Education programme, where children called 'swachhata doots' spread awareness; and Nagaland's 'communitisation' (from 2002) — sharing management of schools, health and electricity with the community.

Every State has a High Court (one may serve several States — Guwahati High Court serves seven north-eastern States). It has a Chief Justice and judges appointed by the President, who consults the Chief Justice of India (and, for judges, the High Court Chief Justice and the Governor). Qualifications: citizen; 10 years in a judicial office in India, or 10 years as an advocate of a High Court. Judges retire at 65 and can be removed only by impeachment by Parliament for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Jurisdiction: original (enforcing Fundamental Rights through writs, election petitions) and appellate (appeals from district courts; confirms death sentences); it supervises subordinate courts and is a court of record. Subordinate courts at district level: civil courts (property, contracts, divorce — no punishment), criminal courts (theft, murder — punishment), and revenue courts (Board of Revenue, Commissioner, Collector, Tehsildar).

vsa: Describe two main functions of the Chief Minister.

(1) The Chief Minister advises the Governor on appointing ministers, allocates portfolios, presides over the Council of Ministers and coordinates ministers. (2) He/she is the sole link between the Council of Ministers and the Governor, communicating all decisions and legislative proposals, and guides the State's policies.
Describe any two legislative powers of a Governor.

(1) The Governor summons and prorogues the State Legislature, can dissolve the Assembly and addresses it. (2) A bill passed by the legislature becomes law only with his/her assent; he/she may return an ordinary bill or reserve it for the President, and nominates one-sixth of the Legislative Council.
Explain any two qualifications for a Governor of an Indian State.

(1) He/she must be a citizen of India and at least 35 years old. (2) He/she must not hold any office of profit; a member of Parliament, a State Legislature or a Council of Ministers who becomes Governor must give up that seat.

or: Explain any two powers of the Chief Minister of a State.

(1) He/she forms the Council of Ministers by advising the Governor and allocates and can change portfolios. (2) He/she guides policy-making, presides over cabinet meetings and is the link between the Governor and the Council of Ministers.

vsa: Which qualifications are required to be a judge of a High Court? Explain any two.

(1) The person must be a citizen of India. (2) He/she must have held a judicial office in India for at least 10 years, or have been an advocate of one or more High Courts for at least 10 years continuously.
Differentiate between civil cases and criminal cases.

Civil cases are disputes between persons about property, contracts, divorce or tenancy; the court settles them and awards no punishment. Criminal cases involve crimes like theft, robbery or murder; the police file them on behalf of the State and the guilty are punished.
sa: Describe any three executive powers of the Governor of a State.

(1) He/she appoints the Chief Minister — the leader of the majority in the Assembly — and other ministers on the CM's advice. (2) He/she appoints the Advocate General and the chairpersons and members of the State Public Service Commission, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission, and judges of courts below the High Court. (3) He/she is consulted on the appointment of High Court judges; all executive action is taken in his/her name, though on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
Explain the executive and legislative powers of the Governor.

Executive: appoints the Chief Minister and ministers, the Advocate General and heads of the State PSC, Election and Finance Commissions; executive power is exercised in his/her name. Legislative: summons and prorogues the legislature and dissolves the Assembly, addresses it, nominates members to the Council (and earlier one Anglo-Indian to the Assembly), and gives assent to bills, returns them or reserves them for the President.
'The Chief Minister is the head of the government in the State and plays a very important role.' Support with examples.

(1) He/she chooses ministers and allocates portfolios (e.g. who handles education or police). (2) He/she presides over the Council of Ministers, coordinates departments and guides policies and bills such as welfare schemes. (3) He/she communicates all decisions to the Governor and is praised or blamed for everything that happens in the State; with a clear majority he/she is very powerful, though in a coalition partners limit the role.
Describe the legislative functions of the State Legislature.

(1) It makes laws on State subjects; ordinary bills may start in either house, but if the Assembly re-passes a bill the Council cannot block it. (2) Money bills start only in the Assembly; the Council must return them within 14 days and the Assembly's decision is final. (3) Passed bills go to the Governor, who cannot refuse a money bill but may return or reserve others for the President.
Explain the functions of the State Legislature.

(1) Legislative — makes laws on State subjects and passes the budget. (2) Control over the executive — the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Assembly and can be removed by a no-confidence motion; questions and adjournment motions keep a check. (3) Electoral — elected MLAs vote for the President and elect Rajya Sabha members and one-third of the Legislative Council; it also ratifies certain constitutional amendments.
Explain the jurisdiction of a High Court.

(1) Original jurisdiction: enforcing Fundamental Rights and other legal rights through writs, and hearing election petitions against members of the State Legislature. (2) Appellate jurisdiction: hearing appeals against judgments of district judges in civil cases and sessions courts in criminal cases (over seven years' imprisonment); confirming death sentences. (3) Supervision: it controls subordinate courts, is a court of record and can punish for contempt.
la: Explain the powers and position of the Governor of a State.

(1) Executive powers: appoints the Chief Minister and ministers, the Advocate General and heads of State commissions. (2) Legislative powers: summons, prorogues and dissolves the legislature, addresses it, nominates members, and assents to or returns bills or reserves them for the President. (3) Financial powers: the budget is presented on his/her behalf, no money bill without recommendation, controls the Contingency Fund. (4) Discretionary powers: chooses the CM when no party has a majority, reserves bills for the President, and reports for President's Rule under Article 356. (5) Position: normally a nominal head who acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the CM. (6) But he/she becomes effective in political instability and as the link between the Centre and the State, so is more than a ceremonial head.
Explain the composition of the State Legislature and how it keeps control over the executive.

(1) It consists of the Governor and one house (Legislative Assembly) or two houses (Assembly and Legislative Council). (2) The Assembly has 60–500 directly elected members for five years; MLAs must be 25. (3) The Council (not more than one-third of the Assembly, at least 40) is permanent: one-third elected by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers, one-sixth nominated; members serve six years. Control: (4) the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Assembly and must resign if a no-confidence motion is passed; (5) members ask questions and supplementary questions, move adjournment motions and calling-attention notices; (6) no bill or budget can pass without the Assembly's approval.
